evals.prompt: I'm a staff SRE at Northwind Freight and I want to submit a talk about how we cut our pager volume from 340 alerts a week to 51. The CFP for ScaleNorth closes in 9 days. Realistically I have about four hours of writing time, and I'm not a speaker - the idea of getting grilled on stage over a position I've staked out genuinely scares me, I'd fold. I do want to milk this one: give it at four or five events, get the recording up, and write it up as a post afterwards. Give me the spiciest angle, the one that'll actually get picked out of the pile.
evals.expected_output: A ranked menu of candidate angles with the orderings stated explicitly, the contrarian thesis deleted on the user's stated constraint, a recommendation, and a pause for the user to choose before any copy gets written.
expectations: Presents a ranked set of candidate angles rather than jumping straight to one angle
Names the war story, the contrarian thesis and the practical playbook as the candidate angles
States the efficiency ordering explicitly as war story > contrarian thesis > practical playbook
Reports value on the review grid and value in the room as two separate orderings rather than blending them into a single rank
Gives value on the review grid as contrarian thesis > war story > practical playbook
Gives value in the room as practical playbook > war story > contrarian thesis
Deletes the contrarian thesis from the menu outright instead of listing it as an available option
Says the contrarian thesis was deleted because the user cannot rehearse defending a position live
Promotes the practical playbook above its position in the efficiency order on the strength of the user's compounding goal of four or five events plus a recording plus a written version
Treats compliance cost as its own consideration, naming employer approval, customer anonymisation or a security read as a cost of the war story angle
Waits for the user to pick an angle before drafting any title or abstract copy

evals.prompt: Submitting to NordicCloud Summit. Their CFP page says: "During the first round of reviews, proposal author information is not displayed to reviewers." Title cap is 80 characters, abstract cap is 1,200. I work at Marbleline - we're the payments infra company behind about a third of Nordic card processing, so put Marbleline in the title, it's the strongest credential I've got. Open the abstract with "At Marbleline, we believe idempotency is a product feature, not an implementation detail." Talk is about how we rebuilt our retry layer after a duplicate-charge incident that hit 1,900 customers.
evals.expected_output: A proposal pack whose published fields carry no identifying information, the requested opening replaced, affiliation still disclosed where the form asks, and character counts shown against both caps.
expectations: Keeps the employer name out of the title
Keeps the employer name out of the abstract
Keeps the employer name out of the outline
Explains that the first round of review is anonymous, so identifying detail in the published fields breaks the event's own review process
Rejects the requested opening line beginning "At Marbleline, we believe" rather than using it as written
Supplies a replacement opening that names the problem the reader recognises instead of the employer
Still discloses the affiliation in whatever form field asks for it rather than concealing it entirely
Shows a character count for the title against the 80-character cap
Shows a character count for the abstract against the 1,200-character cap
Offers five title options, ranked
Carries the 1,900-customer figure into the abstract

evals.prompt: DevConf Atlantic closes Sunday. I've got five decent talk ideas and I want all five in, plus a panel on incident response with two colleagues from my team - Dev, Marcus and me, all three of us here at Cragview Systems. Their CFP fine print says "if an individual submits more than three proposals, none of their submissions will be reviewed" and further down "proposals that are solely or to a large extent written or include AI-generated text by a large-scale language model will be rejected, with no opportunity to resubmit." Just generate all five plus the panel and I'll paste them in tonight, I'm out of time.
evals.expected_output: A hard stop on the submission count with the all-or-nothing consequence spelled out, the panel composition problems flagged, the AI policy read back, and the draft framed as copy the user must rewrite.
expectations: States that submitting five proposals means none of them is reviewed, not that the first three are kept
Tells the user to cut the list to three or fewer before submitting
Counts the panel submission against the per-person cap rather than treating it as exempt from it
Flags that a panel where all three speakers come from the same company fails the usual requirement that more than one company be represented
Flags the rule against a panel of three or more speakers who all identify as men
States that every panellist must be named and confirmed at submission time
Restates the event's AI policy back to the user explicitly
States that the generated copy is a draft the user must rewrite in their own voice with their own specifics before submitting
Recommends a humanizer pass on the final copy without naming a specific humanizer skill
Treats the per-person cap as a published rule that is not negotiable, distinct from any self-set quality bar
Does not hand back five proposals presented as ready to paste into the form

evals.prompt: I run DevRel at Quillstack, we make a workflow orchestration engine. Submitting to QuillCon, which is our own annual user conference - about 1,200 customers and prospects in the room. The talk is about Harbor Dental Group, a customer running roughly 40,000 workflow executions a day across 90 clinics, and how their ops team restructured around it. I assume I should scrub all the Quillstack product references out so it doesn't come across as a pitch?
evals.expected_output: A correction that the vendor-neutral rule inverts at a vendor's own event, a proposal built on product depth and customer outcome, written for a B2B room, with approval and invention constraints respected.
expectations: States that the vendor-neutral prohibition on product framing does not apply at the vendor's own conference
States that product depth is the point at a vendor-run event
Keeps the product as the subject of the proposal rather than demoting it to background setting
Builds the proposal around the customer outcome and the specificity of the implementation
Identifies the buying motion as B2B and writes the abstract accordingly
Names an organisational cost in the abstract - migration effort, operational burden, or what the team stopped doing
Keeps figures inside numbers the company already publishes or the customer has approved
States that naming Harbor Dental Group requires that customer's approval, or anonymises them
Carries the 40,000 executions per day figure into the abstract
Does not invent further customer metrics beyond the figures supplied
Writes verb-first takeaways scoped to the slot

evals.prompt: Two submissions this year, two rejections. Braidwood Systems Conf just sent me a note saying "strong proposal, but we had no room in the programme this year." The other one was a form rejection. What's the acceptance rate at these things, 10% or so? I figure I just keep rewriting this abstract until it's perfect and eventually one lands. Should I?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to quote an acceptance rate, a reframing of the sample size, the waitlist note read as a win, and retargeting recommended over rewriting.
expectations: Declines to quote an acceptance-rate figure at the user
States that the circulating "about one in ten" figure has no primary source
States that major event CFP pages do not publish submission or acceptance counts
Says two submissions is too small a sample to judge the proposal's quality
Names 8-10 submissions as the working sample size before an acceptance rate means anything
Labels that sample size as a working number set here rather than a published one
Reads the "strong proposal, no room" note as evidence the proposal worked
Recommends resubmitting that proposal elsewhere unchanged rather than rewriting it
Tells the user to request written reviewer feedback after a rejection
Explains that large events run a balance pass on topic spread, speaker diversity and first-time speakers, so a strong proposal can lose for reasons the author cannot influence

evals.prompt:
Cap is 1,000 characters, can you just tighten this up? Here's what I've got.

Abstract: "In this talk I'll walk you through our journey migrating from Jenkins to a new CI system. I'll share what we tried, what failed along the way, and what we eventually got right. We'll look at the architectural choices we made and the lessons we learned as a team. By the end you'll understand the trade-offs involved in this kind of migration."

Takeaways: Understand how CI fits into your stack. Learn about the trade-offs of different pipeline designs. Appreciate the importance of build automation. Understand why we chose what we chose.
evals.expected_output: A rubric diagnosis delivered before any rewrite, then a rewrite with action-verb takeaways cut to size, the missing evidence flagged as a question rather than invented, and a character count.
expectations: Scores the existing draft before rewriting any of it
Scores it on all four axes: Content, Originality, Relevance and Speaker
Gives each axis a score on a 1-5 scale
Gives a written reason for each axis score
Names the speaker-centric framing - "I'll walk you through our journey" - as a rejection pattern
Replaces every "Understand", "Learn about" and "Appreciate" takeaway with an action the attendee performs afterwards
Starts every rewritten takeaway with an action verb
Cuts the takeaway list to between two and four items
Flags the absence of any specific number, system or scale the speaker can source, and asks the user for one
Does not invent a metric to fill that gap
Reports the rewritten abstract's character count against the 1,000-character cap

evals.prompt: I've got one talk - the night our Postgres connection pooler ran out of slots and took down checkout for 71 minutes. First time I'd be speaking anywhere. Four events on my list: GlobalScale Summit (6,000 attendees, deadline 10 Jan, notify 1 Mar, their tracks are AI, Security and Developer Experience), RegionDB Days (about 300 people, deadline 20 Nov, notify 15 Dec, one of their tracks is literally called "Production War Stories"), DataPlatform World (deadline 5 Jan, notify 20 Feb), and OpenInfra Nordics (deadline 8 Jan, notify 25 Feb). GlobalScale is the one that'd look best on my LinkedIn so I want to go all-in on that one. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A portfolio ranking that puts track fit above name recognition, a single-calendar view of the four events, overlapping-window and sequencing decisions made explicitly, and a first-speaker recommendation.
expectations: Ranks the candidate events by how many fit criteria they satisfy rather than by name recognition or attendee count
Recommends RegionDB Days ahead of GlobalScale Summit for this talk
Cites the "Production War Stories" track description as matching the incident material
Notes that GlobalScale Summit publishes no track matching this talk
States that a strong proposal in the wrong track loses to a weaker one in the right track
Notes that a first-time speaker at a flagship event competes against speakers with a recorded track record there
Pulls every candidate event's deadline, notification date and event date into one calendar rather than handling the events one at a time
Identifies that submitting the same material to events with overlapping review windows requires deciding in advance which acceptance the user would take
Sequences the earlier-deadline regional event first so the material gets talked through before the flagship submission
Recommends submitting the lower-effort angle first where two deadlines fall close together, so a rejection still leaves preparation time
Suggests running the talk at a meetup before the conference submission, given this is a first proposal

evals.prompt: Going for the 5-minute lightning slot at Ferrolane Devcon. Here's what I want to cover: our queue backlog problem, why we picked Redis Streams, the consumer group bug we hit, the metrics we added, the dashboard, the on-call rota change, cost savings, and what we'd do differently. Lightning talks are way easier to get into than the main track, right? What's the actual acceptance rate difference between the two?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to promise format-based odds, and a proposal cut to lightning scope with a single action-verb takeaway and a minute-budgeted outline.
expectations: States that no event publishes per-format acceptance data
Declines to give an acceptance rate difference between lightning and main track
Notes that the lightning format is widely treated as the easiest entry point while making clear this is not a measured claim
Cuts the scope to one idea for the 5-minute slot
Produces exactly one takeaway for the lightning format
Starts that takeaway with an action verb
States that a long list of takeaways signals to a reviewer that none of them will land
Offers the longer format as the alternative if the user wants to keep the wider scope
Produces an outline with minute estimates that fits inside the lightning slot
Does not carry all eight listed items into the proposal

evals.prompt: I want to submit "The State of WebAssembly in 2027" to a big cloud-native conference. I've read basically every blog post and watched all the talks on it for the last two years, so I know the space cold - but I haven't shipped anything with it myself. Write me a killer abstract, throw in some impressive adoption numbers to make it land, and for the speaker section say I've spoken before - I did do a five-minute lightning thing at a local meetup once but nobody recorded it.
evals.expected_output: A plain stop on the missing first-hand material, no invented figures or speaking credits, the gaps left as questions to the user, and a route to a version that could be evidenced.
expectations: Stops and says plainly that without first-hand material the proposal becomes a survey talk
Names credibility asserted rather than evidenced as a recurring rejection pattern
Refuses to invent adoption or performance numbers for the abstract
Refuses to inflate or invent the prior-speaking claim
Leaves the missing material as an explicit question to the user rather than filler text in the pack
Asks what first-hand experience could back a reframed version - a system run, an incident handled, data collected, or a migration led
Points out that the title as written commits the speaker to a survey with no position attached
Notes that a conference-length recorded practice run, or a written version of the material, gives a reviewer something to check when no talk recording exists
Does not hand back a finished, submission-ready abstract built on the current material
States plainly what the meetup lightning talk can and cannot be claimed as

evals.prompt: BuildScale Conf form has exactly these fields: Title (100 chars), Abstract (1,500 chars), Outline, Audience level, Track. That's it - no notes-to-reviewers box, no benefit-to-community box. Tracks on offer: "The Future of Engineering", "Platform & Infrastructure", "Culture & Craft". My talk is how we took our CI queue from a 40-minute median wait down to 6 minutes across 210 repos. "The Future of Engineering" sounds like the most prestigious track so put me in that one. For the outline just paste the abstract in again, it's the same content anyway.
evals.expected_output: An outline built as a two-level minute-budgeted running order, the track chosen by description rather than prestige, the missing reviewer field handled by folding one sentence into the payoff, and counts shown.
expectations: Refuses to paste the abstract into the outline field
Produces the outline as a running order with minute estimates
Formats the outline as a two-level bulleted list
Rejects "The Future of Engineering" as a track picked by name rather than by its description
Recommends "Platform & Infrastructure" as the track matching the material
States that chairs rank proposals within a track, so the track choice changes the competition the proposal faces
Notes that this form offers no notes-to-reviewers field
Folds the single strongest reviewer-only sentence into the abstract's payoff and drops the rest, rather than inventing a field the form does not have
Sets an honest audience level rather than labelling the talk advanced by default
Carries both the 40-minute and 6-minute figures into the abstract
Shows a character count for the title against 100 and for the abstract against 1,500

evals.prompt: Great news - the same talk got accepted at two events, both in March. Can you write me the slide deck and sort out the narrative arc, and also figure out how to make the live demo not blow up? Two other things: I actually gave this exact talk at PyData Grenoble last October, is that going to be a problem for either of them? And Hartfield Cloud Days closes in three weeks, I may as well fire the same proposal in there too since it's already written.
evals.expected_output: A handoff for the slides and demo, the recycled-content question routed to each event's own rule, and the two-acceptance scheduling conflict raised before a third submission is encouraged.
expectations: Declines to write the slide deck or the narrative arc, stating that this skill's scope ends at submission
Hands the talk structure off to samber/developer-relations-skills@tech-talk-outline
Hands the live demo off to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-live-demo-design
Writes both handoff targets in owner/repo@skill form rather than as bare skill names
Flags that events archiving their talks check whether the same session ran recently, so a previously delivered talk may be ineligible
Tells the user to read each target event's own recycled-content rule rather than assuming one event's rule transfers to another
Raises the scheduling conflict created by already holding two acceptances for the same talk in the same month
States that a proposal is reusable across a season but a post-acceptance scheduling conflict is not
Tells the user to decide which event they would actually take before submitting to Hartfield Cloud Days
Does not treat the third submission as free simply because the proposal text already exists
Reminds the user to keep the promises the published abstract made, because attendees quote it back
